issues.explanation: The trigger pattern is only partly coherent with the trauma type and the rest of the profile. Nausea and visible injuries fit partner physical abuse, but darkness is a more context-specific trigger that is not supported by the memory or appraisal items; no item suggests assaults occurring in dark spaces or fear linked to darkness specifically.

issues.item: Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Public Transport: Using public transport
issues.explanation: Avoiding public transport is hard to explain from the rest of the profile. None of the trigger, memory, or appraisal items point to buses/trains/crowds/public transit as trauma-linked cues, so this strategy appears to target a symptom context not otherwise represented in the profile.

issues.item: Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men
issues.explanation: For trauma type 'physical abuse by romantic partner,' the trigger 'being alone with men' is hard to reconcile unless the abusive partner was male and the fear generalized specifically to men; demographics/trauma description do not support that specificity, so this item is clinically questionable.

issues.item: Negative Appraisals: Mistrust: People can't be trusted
issues.explanation: The appraisal 'People can't be trusted' is very broad and non-specific, while the trigger pattern is specifically male-coded. That combination is not impossible, but here it weakens coherence because the profile gives no corresponding trauma-linked reason for a male-specific trigger alongside a fully generalized interpersonal belief.

Within the Memory node, 'hard to deliberately recall' and 'memories are very clear and detailed' can coexist in PTSD, but in this profile they are phrased in a way that risks direct contradiction unless the distinction between involuntary vivid intrusions and impaired voluntary recall is explicit. A clinician would likely question whether these two items were selected to describe the same memory pattern without additional clarification.

vignette:
Marcus is a twenty-six-year-old detective who has been married for three years, but the life he lives now feels nothing like the one he had before the night his wife, Elena, turned on him. The event itself was sudden and shocking: after an evening of drinking, she accused him of hiding something, and when he tried to leave the room, she grabbed him by the collar, threw him against the wall, and then struck him repeatedly across the face and ribs. He did not fight back; he stood frozen, stunned, as her fists connected. The smell of wine on her breath mixed with the metallic taste of blood in his mouth, and the sight of his own blood on her knuckles became an image he has never been able to shake. In the weeks that followed, Elena apologized, swore it would never happen again, and Marcus told himself it was a one-time mistake. But the memory of that night did not fade. It remained vivid and detailed, as though burned directly into his mind-he could still hear her voice, the exact pitch of her accusation, the sound of his own head hitting the wall. And the memory forced its way into his awareness without warning, often when he was trying to focus on work or relax at home.

Marcus works as a detective in a busy precinct, and his daily environment is saturated with potential triggers. When he interviews victims of domestic violence, the visible bruises on their faces or arms immediately pull him back to that night, the memory rising unbidden with full sensory force. He has also come to dread the smell of alcohol on anyone-colleagues after a shift, witnesses in interrogation rooms-because the odor alone is enough to send him reeling into a flash of that moment, the nausea climbing in his throat. These triggers do not just evoke the memory; they also reinforce what he has come to believe about the world. He has lost his faith in people, in life, in anything resembling safety. He feels like a permanent outsider now, watching others interact with trust he can no longer imagine. He is convinced that people are not what they seem, that anyone can turn violent without warning. When the nausea rises or he sees an injury on someone else, these appraisals solidify-this is the real truth, he thinks, and the rest is just a mask.

To manage the intrusion of the memory and the weight of these beliefs, Marcus has developed a set of strategies that have slowly reshaped his entire existence. He avoids relaxing because relaxation feels dangerous-a state of vigilance is the only thing that keeps him safe. At home, he paces, he checks the locks twice, he stays alert to Elena's mood. He has also begun to numb his feelings deliberately, shutting down emotionally during conversations, especially if they touch on anything personal. And he avoids being touched. Any form of physical contact-a hand on his shoulder from a colleague, Elena reaching for his arm in bed-makes his skin crawl and his heart race. These strategies have consequences. His marriage is strained; Elena has started to ask why he flinches when she comes near, and he cannot explain. At work, his captain has noticed he is withdrawn, less collaborative, and Marcus has started to request only solo assignments.

The cycle tightens. The more he numbs and avoids, the more isolated he feels, and the isolation feeds his sense of being an outsider, his distrust deepening. The numbing also means he does not process the memory, so it remains vivid and uncontrolled, ready to be triggered again by the next smell of alcohol or sight of a bruise. The avoidance of touch and relaxation, meanwhile, keeps his body in a state of low-grade hyperarousal, which makes him more sensitive to somatic triggers like nausea, which in turn pulls him back into the memory. He has become trapped in a loop where every strategy meant to protect him only strengthens the very things he is trying to escape.

Marcus finally came to therapy after a day at work when he interviewed a woman with a black eye and had to excuse himself to vomit in the bathroom. He realized he could no longer do his job, and he could no longer live this way. What frightens him most is the possibility that he will never trust anyone again-not his wife, not his colleagues, not himself. He is hoping, quietly, that there might be a way back to the person he was before that night, though he is not sure he believes it is possible.
